# A query is a claim about the answer.

A SQL query can be syntactically valid and still answer the wrong question. Writing the query is therefore only part of the work. We must also predict its result and construct cases that distinguish the intended meaning from plausible mistakes. The relational-algebra ideas from Week 2 now become practical: SQL is the language we write, but the meaning still comes from the logical operations the query expresses.

:::

**Previous:** [Changing table data with SQL](week-04-changing-table-data.qmd)

## 1. Our relation for today

We will use the **video game platform database** from [Defining tables with PostgreSQL](week-03-defining-relations-with-sql.qmd). Its `player_account` and `video_game` tables describe players and games; today we query the `save_file` relation from that lecture's save-file practice.

**One row represents one saved game belonging to a player.** A player can have several saves, including several for the same game. We begin with one relation so each clause has a visible purpose; joins and aggregation come later.

$$
\text{save\_file}(\text{save\_id},\ \text{player\_id},\ \text{game\_id},\ \text{saved\_at},\ \text{completion\_percent},\ \text{slot\_label})
$$

| save_id | player_id | game_id | saved_at | completion_percent | slot_label |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 2026-09-24 09:00-06 | 25.00 | `NULL` |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 2026-09-24 10:00-06 | 50.00 | `NULL` |
| 3 | 2 | 1 | 2026-09-24 09:00-06 | 49.99 | favorite |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 2026-09-24 11:00-06 | 75.00 | `NULL` |
| 5 | 3 | 2 | 2026-09-24 09:00-06 | 80.00 | `NULL` |
| 6 | 3 | 2 | 2026-09-24 10:00-06 | 100.00 | favorite |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 2026-09-24 10:00-06 | `NULL` | new run |
| 8 | 2 | 3 | 2026-09-24 11:00-06 | 80.00 | `NULL` |

`completion_percent` is `numeric(5, 2)`: `50.00` means 50% complete, and `NULL` means the game has not reported progress. It does **not** mean zero. Known values range from 0 through 100. A missing `slot_label` means the save is unnamed. Timestamps here include a UTC offset of −06; your database client may display the same instants in another time zone.

<details class="practice-example">
<summary>Runnable PostgreSQL setup: a fresh instance of our game database</summary>

Run this block once in your personal schema. These regular tables use the definitions from the schema lecture and remain after you disconnect.

- The examples assume newly created tables so the generated IDs match the sample data below. If tables with these names already exist, inspect them and save any data you need before dropping and recreating them.
- You can keep these tables for later practice. If you choose to drop them when finished, drop `save_file` before `player_account` and `video_game` because it references both. Reconnecting does not reset the tables.

```sql
CREATE TABLE video_game (
    game_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    title text NOT NULL,
    studio_name text NOT NULL,
    released_on date,
    is_available boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true
);

CREATE TABLE player_account (
    player_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    username text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    account_status text NOT NULL
        CHECK (account_status IN ('active', 'suspended', 'closed'))
);

CREATE TABLE save_file (
    save_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    player_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES player_account(player_id),
    game_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES video_game(game_id),
    saved_at timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,
    completion_percent numeric(5, 2)
        CHECK (completion_percent BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
    slot_label text
);

INSERT INTO video_game (title, studio_name, released_on)
VALUES
    ('Starfall Cartographers', 'Northline Studio', DATE '2024-10-04'),
    ('Mosslight', 'Juniper Byte', NULL),
    ('Circuit Garden', 'Northline Studio', DATE '2026-02-12');

INSERT INTO player_account (username, account_status)
VALUES ('pixel_fox', 'active'), ('moss_runner', 'active'), ('star_mapper', 'active');

-- In this fresh setup, generated player and game IDs are 1, 2, and 3.
INSERT INTO save_file
    (player_id, game_id, saved_at, completion_percent, slot_label)
VALUES
    (1, 1, '2026-09-24 09:00-06', 25.00, NULL),
    (1, 1, '2026-09-24 10:00-06', 50.00, NULL),
    (2, 1, '2026-09-24 09:00-06', 49.99, 'favorite'),
    (1, 1, '2026-09-24 11:00-06', 75.00, NULL),
    (3, 2, '2026-09-24 09:00-06', 80.00, NULL),
    (3, 2, '2026-09-24 10:00-06', 100.00, 'favorite'),
    (2, 3, '2026-09-24 10:00-06', NULL, 'new run'),
    (2, 3, '2026-09-24 11:00-06', 80.00, NULL);
```

The remaining queries only read these rows, so their predictions stay consistent throughout the lecture.

</details>

::: {.callout-question appearance="simple"}
## Predict before querying

How many saves report at least 50% completion? Which save tests whether “at least” was translated correctly?
:::

## 2. The basic query shape

Imagine building a page where players can browse their saved games. We begin with information someone wants to see, decide what belongs in the result, and then express that request in SQL.

**Question:** Which saves are at least halfway through the game, and when were they saved? Show the save time and completion percentage for every save at least 50% complete.

A small SQL query expresses this request with three central clauses:

```sql
SELECT saved_at, completion_percent
FROM save_file
WHERE completion_percent >= 50;
```

Read the clauses as answers to three questions:

| Clause | Question it answers | Relational connection |
|---|---|---|
| `FROM save_file` | Which relation supplies the tuples? | Input relation |
| `WHERE completion_percent >= 50` | Which tuples qualify? | Selection, $\sigma$ |
| `SELECT saved_at, completion_percent` | Which expressions appear in the result? | Projection, $\pi$ |

SQL writes `SELECT` first, but a useful conceptual reading is:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["FROM<br/>begin with save_file"] --> B["WHERE<br/>keep qualifying tuples"]
    B --> C["SELECT<br/>form result attributes"]
    C --> D["ORDER BY<br/>arrange the display, if requested"]

    classDef input fill:#f7f3ea,stroke:#9b7b36,color:#3f321c;
    classDef operation fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    classDef display fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    class A input;
    class B,C operation;
    class D display;
```

This is a learning model, not a complete specification of SQL's logical-processing rules. It is enough to reason about today's queries.

### The predicted result

| saved_at | completion_percent |
|---|---:|
| 2026-09-24 10:00-06 | 50.00 |
| 2026-09-24 11:00-06 | 75.00 |
| 2026-09-24 09:00-06 | 80.00 |
| 2026-09-24 10:00-06 | 100.00 |
| 2026-09-24 11:00-06 | 80.00 |

The table shows the qualifying values, but its row order is not guaranteed because the query did not request one.

## 3. Selection chooses tuples

The `WHERE` clause evaluates a predicate for each candidate tuple. A tuple remains in the result when the predicate evaluates to `TRUE`.

**Question:** What saved games does `pixel_fox` have? In our sample data, this player's ID is 1. Return every attribute for their saves so we can inspect the full records.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM save_file
WHERE player_id = 1;
```

The asterisk asks for all available attributes. It can be useful during exploration, but named attributes usually communicate a result contract more clearly.

### Comparisons

| SQL operator | Meaning |
|:---:|---|
| `=` | equal |
| `<>` or `!=` | not equal |
| `<`, `<=` | less than, at most |
| `>`, `>=` | greater than, at least |
| `BETWEEN a AND b` | within an inclusive range |

**Question:** Which saves are between one-quarter and three-quarters complete? Show each qualifying save's ID and completion percentage, including saves exactly 25% or 75% complete.

```sql
SELECT save_id, completion_percent
FROM save_file
WHERE completion_percent BETWEEN 25 AND 75;
```

`BETWEEN 25 AND 75` includes both 25 and 75. Boundary values are therefore particularly valuable tests.

::: {.activity-checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** How would the result differ if the requirement said “more than 80% complete” rather than “at least 80% complete”? Which sample rows make the two predicates distinguishable?
:::

### Combining predicates

**Question:** Which of `pixel_fox`'s saves are at least halfway complete? Show the save ID, save time, and completion percentage. A save must belong to player 1 and be at least 50% complete.

```sql
SELECT save_id, saved_at, completion_percent
FROM save_file
WHERE player_id = 1
  AND completion_percent >= 50;
```

The logical connectives are:

- `AND`: both conditions must hold;
- `OR`: at least one condition must hold; and
- `NOT`: reverse a condition's truth value, subject to SQL's handling of `NULL`.

**Question:** Which of `star_mapper`'s saves are favorites or nearly finished? This player's ID is 3; “nearly finished” means at least 80% complete, and a favorite has the label `favorite`. Show the save ID, player ID, completion percentage, and label.

Parentheses make that grouping explicit:

```sql
SELECT save_id, player_id, completion_percent, slot_label
FROM save_file
WHERE player_id = 3
  AND (slot_label = 'favorite' OR completion_percent >= 80);
```

This returns saves **5 and 6**, both belonging to `star_mapper`. Save 8 is also 80% complete, but belongs to `moss_runner` (player 2), so it must be excluded.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## English “and” and “or” can hide ambiguity

We want `player 3 AND (favorite OR nearly complete)`. Without parentheses, the query below instead asks for **player 3's favorites or any player's nearly complete saves**:

```sql
SELECT save_id, player_id, completion_percent, slot_label
FROM save_file
WHERE player_id = 3
  AND slot_label = 'favorite' OR completion_percent >= 80;
```

SQL evaluates `AND` before `OR`, so this means `(player 3 AND favorite) OR nearly complete`. It returns saves **5, 6, and 8**. Save 8 exposes the mistake: its 80% completion lets it through even though it belongs to player 2.
:::

## 4. Projection shapes the result

Projection is not merely hiding columns from a display. It defines which expressions and attribute names belong to the query result.

**Question:** How far along is each saved game? Show every save's ID and completion percentage, including saves whose progress is unknown.

```sql
SELECT save_id, completion_percent
FROM save_file;
```

### Expressions create derived values

**Question:** How much progress remains for each save, and what fraction is complete? Return one row per save with its ID, reported percentage, percentage points remaining, and completed fraction.

SQL expressions calculate these values without altering the stored relation:

```sql
SELECT
    save_id,
    completion_percent,
    100 - completion_percent AS remaining_percent,
    completion_percent / 100.0 AS completion_fraction
FROM save_file;
```

`remaining_percent` and `completion_fraction` are **aliases** for derived result attributes. No columns are added to `save_file`, and no stored values change. At 75% completion, 25 percentage points remain; the completed fraction is 0.75.

| save_id | completion_percent | remaining_percent | completion_fraction |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 25.00 | 75.00 | 0.25 |
| 2 | 50.00 | 50.00 | 0.50 |
| 3 | 49.99 | 50.01 | 0.4999 |
| 4 | 75.00 | 25.00 | 0.75 |
| 5 | 80.00 | 20.00 | 0.80 |
| 6 | 100.00 | 0.00 | 1.00 |
| 7 | `NULL` | `NULL` | `NULL` |
| 8 | 80.00 | 20.00 | 0.80 |

Trailing zeros may differ in your client's display. The values above are exact. Arithmetic with unreported progress also produces `NULL`.

### Math can appear in selection, too

**Question:** Which saves have at most 20 percentage points remaining? Return the save ID and remaining progress, with the smallest remainder first. Break ties by save ID, lowest first.

```sql
SELECT save_id, 100 - completion_percent AS remaining_percent
FROM save_file
WHERE 100 - completion_percent <= 20
ORDER BY remaining_percent ASC, save_id ASC;
```

| save_id | remaining_percent |
|---:|---:|
| 6 | 0.00 |
| 5 | 20.00 |
| 8 | 20.00 |

The expression in `WHERE` determines **which rows qualify** (selection). The expression in `SELECT` determines **what values we return** (projection with a calculation). The predicate could also be written `completion_percent >= 80`.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## A SELECT alias is not available in the same query's WHERE

Writing `WHERE remaining_percent <= 20` in the query above would fail in PostgreSQL: `remaining_percent` is an output name, not a column of `save_file`. Repeat the expression in `WHERE`. An output alias **can** be used in `ORDER BY`, as shown above.
:::

<details class="practice-example">
<summary>Preview: name a derived field before filtering it</summary>

We want the same result: save IDs and remaining progress for saves with at most 20 percentage points left, ordered by remaining progress and then save ID. This time, we want to name the calculation before filtering it.

A nested query exposes the derived field as an input column for an outer query:

```sql
SELECT save_id, remaining_percent
FROM (
    SELECT save_id, 100 - completion_percent AS remaining_percent
    FROM save_file
) AS progress
WHERE remaining_percent <= 20
ORDER BY remaining_percent ASC, save_id ASC;
```

The inner query forms a table named `progress` for this query. The outer query can filter its `remaining_percent` column. It returns the same three rows as the previous query; we will develop nested queries later.

</details>

### Parentheses and numeric types affect the question

**Question:** Which saves have at most one-fifth of the game left? Show each save's ID and the **fraction remaining**, where `0.20` means 20% remains.

Subtract first, then divide:

```sql
SELECT save_id,
       (100 - completion_percent) / 100.0 AS remaining_fraction
FROM save_file
WHERE (100 - completion_percent) / 100.0 <= 0.20;
```

For save 5, `(100 - 80.00) / 100.0` is `0.20`. Without parentheses, `100 - 80.00 / 100.0` is `99.20`: division occurs before subtraction. The query above returns saves 5, 6, and 8, with fractions 0.20, 0.00, and 0.20, in unspecified order.

**Question:** Does dividing two integers produce the same result as division with a decimal operand? Return one row with both calculations of one-half side by side.

PostgreSQL distinguishes integer division from decimal division:

```sql
SELECT 1 / 2 AS integer_result,
       1 / 2.0 AS decimal_result;
```

The results are `0` and `0.5`. Our `completion_percent` column is already `numeric`; using `100.0` also makes the intended decimal calculation clear.

::: {.activity-checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** Predict the remaining progress for saves 3, 5, 6, and 7. Which save distinguishes `< 20` from `<= 20`? Why does save 7 fail to qualify even though its remaining progress is not known to exceed 20?
:::

### Names are part of the interface

Suppose we want just the percentage points remaining for every save. `SELECT 100 - completion_percent FROM save_file;` returns those values, but gives the result column no meaningful name. Adding `AS remaining_percent` communicates the meaning and unit to people and downstream programs.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## A result is itself tabular

SQL queries return named columns and rows that can be displayed, consumed by an application, nested inside another query, or used to define a view.
:::

## 5. Duplicates: `SELECT` is not automatically set projection

**Question:** Who owns each save? Show only the player ID, keeping one result row per save even when the same player appears repeatedly.

```sql
SELECT player_id
FROM save_file;
```

The result contains eight rows because SQL normally preserves duplicates:

```text
1
1
2
1
3
3
2
2
```

**Question:** Which players have at least one save? Show each represented player ID once, regardless of how many saves that player owns.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT player_id
FROM save_file;
```

```text
1
2
3
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## `DISTINCT` changes the meaning

Do not add `DISTINCT` merely to conceal unexpected duplicates. First decide whether repeated rows represent repeated facts, an incorrect query, or a result in which multiplicity matters.
:::

This is one important difference between classical relational algebra and SQL: mathematical relations are sets, while SQL queries generally use **bag** or **multiset** behavior unless duplicate elimination is requested.

## 6. Ordering is requested, not inherited

**Question:** Which saves are at least 50% complete? Show their IDs and completion percentages, highest completion first. When percentages tie, put the lower save ID first.

```sql
SELECT save_id, completion_percent
FROM save_file
WHERE completion_percent >= 50
ORDER BY completion_percent DESC, save_id ASC;
```

The second ordering expression breaks ties. Without it, rows with equal completion percentages could appear in either order.

| Keyword | Direction |
|---|---|
| `ASC` | ascending; the default when direction is omitted |
| `DESC` | descending |

`ORDER BY` controls the presentation of the query result. It is not part of classical relational algebra because a mathematical relation is unordered.

::: {.activity-checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** Is `ORDER BY save_id` a reliable substitute for `ORDER BY saved_at`? Use saves 2 and 3 to test the assumption that a larger ID always means a later save time.
:::

## 7. `NULL` is not an ordinary value

Save 7 has no reported completion percentage. SQL uses `NULL` to represent missing or inapplicable information, but `NULL` does not behave like a normal number or string.

**Question:** Which saves have no reported progress? Show their IDs and slot labels so we can identify them.

An equality comparison with `NULL` does **not** find those saves:

```sql
WHERE completion_percent = NULL
```

To get the requested saves, use the dedicated `IS NULL` predicate:

```sql
SELECT save_id, slot_label
FROM save_file
WHERE completion_percent IS NULL;
```

### Why equality fails

If `NULL` represents unknown progress, then the truth of “unknown progress equals 80” is itself unknown. The same is true of “unknown progress does not equal 80.”

| Predicate | Result |
|---|---|
| `80 = 80` | `TRUE` |
| `80 = 50` | `FALSE` |
| `NULL = 80` | `UNKNOWN` |
| `NULL <> 80` | `UNKNOWN` |
| `NULL IS NULL` | `TRUE` |

A `WHERE` clause retains only tuples for which its predicate is `TRUE`. Tuples producing `FALSE` or `UNKNOWN` are filtered out.

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple"}
## `NULL` does not explain why a value is absent

A missing completion value might mean progress is not yet reported or the game does not track it. If the distinction matters, represent the reason explicitly rather than asking one marker to carry several meanings.
:::

### Include nearly complete saves or unreported progress

**Question:** Which saves are at least 80% complete or have no reported progress? Show their IDs, completion percentages, and slot labels. Include both groups in the result.

```sql
SELECT save_id, completion_percent, slot_label
FROM save_file
WHERE completion_percent >= 80
   OR completion_percent IS NULL;
```

This query makes the two qualifying cases explicit.

## 8. One question in SQL and algebra

**Question:** Which saves are at least 80% complete? Return their IDs and completion percentages. We will express this same request in SQL and relational algebra.

```sql
SELECT save_id, completion_percent
FROM save_file
WHERE completion_percent >= 80;
```

One relational-algebra expression for the same intention is:

$$
\pi_{\text{save\_id},\ \text{completion\_percent}}
\left(
\sigma_{\text{completion\_percent} \ge 80}(\text{save\_file})
\right)
$$

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["save_file<br/>6 attributes · 8 tuples"] --> B["σ completion_percent ≥ 80<br/>keep qualifying tuples"]
    B --> C["π save_id, completion_percent<br/>keep requested attributes"]
    C --> D["result<br/>2 attributes · 3 tuples"]

    classDef relation fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    classDef operation fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    class A,D relation;
    class B,C operation;
```

The algebra makes the composition visible. The SQL is the practical language we send to the DBMS. Neither representation eliminates the need to test the interpretation.

## 9. Query writing is a testing activity

Suppose the requirement is:

> List each player with a save at least 80% complete, once per player.

A disciplined process is:

### Step 1: State the result contract

- one output attribute: `player_id`;
- one row per qualifying player, not per save;
- include a save exactly 80% complete;
- exclude unreported progress.

### Step 2: Write a candidate

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT player_id
FROM save_file
WHERE completion_percent >= 80;
```

### Step 3: Construct distinguishing cases

| Test row or condition | Mistake it can expose |
|---|---|
| A player's only qualifying save is exactly 80% complete | `>` used instead of `>=` |
| Two qualifying saves for the same player | missing `DISTINCT` |
| A row with `completion_percent IS NULL` | incorrect assumptions about missing values |
| A qualifying save for a second player | query accidentally hard-codes one player |

### Step 4: Predict before executing

For the supplied instance, the expected result contains player IDs **2 and 3**, once each, in unspecified order. Saves 5 and 6 qualify for player 3; save 8 qualifies for player 2.

**A boundary can be hidden by another row.** Changing `>= 80` to `> 80` still returns player 3 because save 6 is 100% complete. But player 2's only qualifying save is exactly 80% complete. Save 8 therefore exposes the mistake: the correct query returns players 2 and 3; the incorrect query returns only player 3.

### Step 5: Compare evidence with the contract

If the result differs, revise either the query or the interpretation. A query that matches one sample by accident is not yet trustworthy.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The best tiny dataset is not necessarily realistic

A useful test dataset contains deliberately chosen duplicates, boundary values, missing values, and near misses. Its job is to distinguish meanings with as few rows as possible.
:::

## 10. A reusable translation routine

When you receive a new question, work through this sequence:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Question and<br/>result contract"] --> B["SQL<br/>candidate"]
    B --> C["Prediction and<br/>boundary cases"]
    C --> D["Execute, compare,<br/>and revise"]

    classDef thought fill:#f7f3ea,stroke:#9b7b36,color:#3f321c;
    classDef query fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    classDef evidence fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    class A thought;
    class B,C query;
    class D evidence;
```

The phrase **define one result row** is especially important. It prevents many later mistakes involving duplicates and aggregation.

::: {.takeaway-panel}
## The main claim

`SELECT`, `FROM`, and `WHERE` are compact, but the real skill is translating a question into a precise result contract and then testing whether the query satisfies it.
:::
